statement: An open-collector (TTL) or open-drain (CMOS) output has no internal high-side device, so a valid HIGH exists only if an external pull-up resistor connects the output node to VCC/VDD; the internal output transistor pulls the node near ground for LOW. The pull-up may return to a rail higher than the logic supply -- typically up to +30 V on an open collector depending on logic family -- which is why OC/OD buffers are used to drive LEDs, lamps, and relays.
condition: Applies to every open-collector or open-drain output pin (gates, buffers, comparators); without the external pull-up the HIGH state is undefined/floating.

values.pullup_destination: VCC/VDD (e.g., +5 V for TTL) or higher load supply
values.totem_pole_sink_limit_for_comparison: IOL(max) 16 mA standard TTL, 8 mA LS TTL

design_notes: Prefer OC/OD over totem-pole/push-pull outputs when the load needs more current or voltage than the logic family's IOL(max)/VCC allows
When driving an LED from an OC output, add a series current-limit resistor; a resistive lamp filament needs none
ANSI/IEEE diamond-with-underbar symbol on a pin marks an OC/OD output; same symbol for both technologies

source.section: 15-3 TTL (Bipolar) Circuits (Open-Collector Gates) + 15-2 CMOS Circuits (Open-Drain Gates); current limits in 15-4 (pdf_page_index 867, 872, 877, 878)

statement: Wired-AND bus: tie N open-collector/open-drain outputs to one node with a single shared pull-up resistor Rp to VCC. The node is LOW whenever any one output transistor is on and HIGH only when all are off, giving X = AND of the individual gate outputs (with inverters as drivers this is a negative-AND: X = /A*/B*/C*/D).
inputs: N logic signals, one per OC/OD gate driving the shared node
outputs: Single shared line X (wired-AND of all driver outputs)
required_blocks: N gates with open-collector or open-drain outputs (e.g., 74LS09 quad 2-input AND with OC outputs)
One pull-up resistor Rp from the shared node to VCC (exactly one per wired-AND net, not one per gate)
condition: Every output on the shared node must be OC/OD; never place a totem-pole/push-pull output on a wired-AND net.
design_notes: A single external Rp is required in all wired-AND circuits; four 2-input OC AND gates wired together create an 8-input AND (X = ABCDEFGH)
Rp minimum value is set by the sink limit of one output transistor: it must carry Rp current plus all driven-input IIL while holding VOL(max) (see wired-and-pullup-sizing-worked)
Node HIGH level is established passively through Rp, so rising transitions are RC-limited by node capacitance

source.section: 15-4 Practical Considerations in the Use of TTL (Using Open-Collector Gates for Wired-AND Operation, Figures 15-37/15-38/15-39)

statement: Minimum shared pull-up resistor for a wired-AND net is computed from the single sinking transistor's current budget: Rp(min) = (VCC - VOL(max)) / (IOL(max) - sum of driven-input IIL).
problem: Three open-collector AND gates wired-AND together (X = ABCDEF) drive four standard TTL inputs (1.6 mA sink each). Find the minimum Rp given IOL(max) = 30 mA per gate and VOL(max) = 0.4 V, VCC = 5 V.
assumptions: Worst case: only one OC output transistor is on and must sink the entire node current
Each standard TTL driven input sources IIL = 1.6 mA into the LOW node
steps: Total load current into the LOW node: 4 x 1.6 mA = 6.4 mA
Current budget left for the pull-up: IRp = IOL(max) - 6.4 mA = 30 mA - 6.4 mA = 23.6 mA
Rp(min) = (VCC - VOL(max)) / IRp = (5 V - 0.4 V) / 23.6 mA = 195 ohm
result: Rp >= 195 ohm (smaller Rp would force the sinking transistor past IOL(max) and raise VOL above 0.4 V)
condition: Wired-AND / open-drain shared line where one output must hold the node at VOL(max) while sinking pull-up plus all load currents.

source.section: 15-4 Practical Considerations in the Use of TTL, Example 15-6 (Figure 15-40)

statement: Condition: two totem-pole (push-pull) outputs are wired to the same node and one drives HIGH while the other drives LOW. Consequence: the HIGH driver's upper transistor is effectively shorted to ground through the LOW driver's saturated lower transistor, producing excessive current that can damage both devices. Totem-pole outputs must never be tied together; use OC/OD wired logic or tri-state outputs for shared lines.
condition: Any direct parallel connection of standard push-pull logic outputs (TTL totem-pole or CMOS complementary pair).
consequence: Excessive shoot-through current from one device's high-side into the other's low-side; possible device destruction.

values.note: No safe current value exists for this connection; Floyd's summary rule is absolute: 'Totem-pole outputs of TTL cannot be connected together'

source.section: 15-4 Practical Considerations in the Use of TTL (Connection of Totem-Pole Outputs, Figure 15-41; chapter summary pdf_page_index 885)

statement: On a shared bus line, at most one tri-state output may be enabled at any given time; every other output on the line must be disabled into the high-impedance (high-Z) state, where it behaves as an open switch disconnected from the line. Devices without built-in tri-state or open-collector outputs must connect to a bus through external tri-state buffers.
condition: Two or more device outputs share any signal line (data bus, address bus, shared control line).

values.enable_polarity: device-specific: active-HIGH or active-LOW enable variants both exist (Figure 13-78); CMOS example in Figure 15-23 enables on LOW, TTL example in Figure 15-33 enables on LOW
values.high_z_mechanism: both output transistors (pull-up and pull-down) turned off simultaneously

design_notes: In the tri-state CMOS inverter, enable HIGH turns off both Q1 and Q2 giving high-Z; enable LOW restores normal logic operation -- always check each part's enable polarity before wiring select logic
Select logic for multiple sources must be mutually exclusive (e.g., one select line with true/inverted enables for a two-source bus)
The inverted-triangle symbol on a pin marks a tri-state output

source.section: 14 Practical Computer System Considerations (Shared Signal Lines) + 13-10 Bus Interfacing + 15-2/15-3 tri-state circuits (pdf_page_index 785-786, 807, 867, 872)

statement: Condition: two or more outputs on a common bus line drive it toward different logic levels because more than one driver is (momentarily) enabled. Consequence: high current flows from one output into the other, which can damage the devices. The most common trigger is enable-timing overlap -- one device has not completely turned off (tri-stated) before the next one turns on, typically at memory READ-to-WRITE turnaround; even two outputs at the same nominal logic level contend because device output voltages differ slightly.
condition: Shared bus line with overlapping driver enables, or any timing window where two drivers are simultaneously active.
consequence: High inter-device current, corrupted bus levels, potential device damage.

values.typical_scenario: memory systems switching between READ and WRITE modes (timing problem)

source.section: 13-10 Bus Interfacing (Bus Contention) + 14 Practical Computer System Considerations (Shared Signal Lines) (pdf_page_index 786 and 807)

statement: Bidirectional bus port: each I/O line connects to the bus through an anti-parallel pair of tri-state buffers with complementary enables driven by one SND/RCV direction line, so exactly one buffer of the pair is ever active. Direction LOW enables the outbound buffer (device drives the bus); direction HIGH enables the inbound buffer (device receives from the bus).
outputs: Bidirectional connection between device port and shared bus, contention-free by construction
required_blocks: Per bus line: two tri-state buffers connected in opposite directions between device pin and bus line
One direction signal with inversion so the two buffer enables are complementary
For multi-source (non-bidirectional) buses: one tri-state buffer bank per source with mutually exclusive selects (select LOW connects source A, HIGH connects source B)
condition: Device with combined input/output port pins that must be multiplexed onto a shared data bus; all other devices on the bus must obey the single-enabled-driver rule.
design_notes: The complementary-enable structure makes simultaneous send and receive impossible on a line, preventing self-contention
Many microprocessors/memories integrate these buffers internally; add external ones only for devices without tri-state outputs

source.section: 13-10 Bus Interfacing (Multiplexed I/Os, Figure 13-80; two-source select, Figure 13-76)

statement: Condition: a slowly changing or noisy signal hovers around the single switching threshold of a standard (non-hysteresis) logic input. Consequence: the device switches erratically, producing multiple spurious output transitions. A Schmitt-trigger input avoids this with hysteresis (separate upper and lower trip points) and triggers reliably even when the input changes as slowly as 1 volt/second.
condition: Slow rise/fall edges (RC-shaped signals, sensor outputs, long lines) or system noise superimposed near the input threshold, feeding a non-Schmitt logic/clock input.
consequence: Erratic switching between states / multiple output transitions per intended edge; downstream counters and flip-flops register false clocks.

source.section: 7-5 One-Shots (The Schmitt-Trigger Symbol) + 14 Practical Computer System Considerations (buffers, pdf_page_index 809)

statement: Insert a Schmitt-trigger buffer or inverter between any slow-changing or noisy signal source and downstream edge-sensitive logic. The hysteresis between the upper trip point (UTP) and lower trip point (LTP) means noise smaller than the hysteresis band cannot re-cross the active threshold, so the output makes exactly one clean transition per input edge.
inputs: Slow or noisy digital-ish signal (RC-filtered line, switch/sensor output, long cable)
outputs: Clean, fast-edged logic signal safe for clocks and edge-triggered inputs
required_blocks: One Schmitt-trigger gate (buffer or inverter; hysteresis-symbol input) per conditioned line
Optional: same Schmitt inverter plus feedback R (output to input) and C (input to ground) forms an astable clock oscillating between UTP and LTP (Figure 7-55)
condition: Use whenever the input slew is too slow or too noisy for a standard input; Schmitt inputs remain reliable down to 1 V/s input slew.
design_notes: Floyd's ch. 14 guidance: Schmitt triggers are one of the standard buffer types used to keep logic devices from acting erratically when system noise affects slowly changing inputs
Hysteresis symbol inside the gate body marks Schmitt inputs on schematics
The Schmitt+RC astable variant produces a square-wave clock without a crystal; frequency set by the RC time constant between UTP and LTP crossings (exact f equation not given in Floyd)

source.section: 7-5 One-Shots (Schmitt-Trigger Symbol, pdf_page_index 417) + 7-6 The Astable Multivibrator (Figure 7-55, pdf_page_index 423) + ch. 14 (pdf_page_index 809)

statement: SPDT switch debouncer: an S-R (NAND) latch with both inputs pulled up to VCC through resistors and an SPDT switch grounding either the S-side or R-side contact. The first contact touch sets (or resets) the latch; all subsequent bounce spikes on that input cannot change the already-latched state, so Q delivers a single clean edge per throw in both directions.
inputs: SPDT (form-C, break-before-make) mechanical switch, common terminal to ground
outputs: Q: bounce-free logic transition (one clean LOW-to-HIGH or HIGH-to-LOW edge per switch throw)
required_blocks: S-R latch (fixed-function example: 74HC279A quad S-R latch)
Two pull-up resistors (R1, R2) from VCC to the latch S and R inputs
SPDT switch: pole to ground, throw 1 to R input node, throw 2 to S input node
condition: Any mechanical switch or pushbutton feeding edge-sensitive logic; bounce lasts long enough that raw contacts produce multiple spikes per actuation.
design_notes: Requires an SPDT (two-throw) switch -- a plain SPST switch cannot use this latch pattern because each throw must ground a different latch input

Alternative time-based approach from Floyd's keyboard-encoder design: a one-shot delays the register-load clock after key closure so contact bounce dies out before data is latched, and simultaneously inhibits the scan counter (pdf_page_index 476)
Bounce spikes are 'very short in duration' but unacceptable to digital systems -- never clock counters/flip-flops directly from raw switch contacts
